title: Budgeting Frameworks

learn.summary: A budget is not a punishment; it's a plan for money that already exists, and research on planning prompts shows written plans measurably change follow-through. The major frameworks — proportional rules like 50/30/20, zero-based allocation, and cash envelopes — all work by the same mechanism: deciding before spending instead of after. The best framework is the one you'll still be using in three months, so fit beats theoretical purity.

do: Pick one framework below, run it on paper against last month's real numbers, and write two sentences on where it fit your life and where it chafed.

children.title: The 50/30/20 Rule

learn.summary: Popularized by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi in 'All Your Worth': after-tax income splits into roughly 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt payments beyond minimums. Its power is diagnostic — sorting your real spending into the three buckets instantly shows whether the strain is fixed costs or lifestyle. In high-cost cities the 50 is often unrealistic, which is information about the housing market, not a personal failing.

do: Sort last month's spending into needs, wants, and savings/extra debt payments, and compute your actual three percentages next to the 50/30/20 benchmark.

children.title: Zero-Based Budgeting

learn.summary: Every dollar of income gets a written job before the month starts — spending, saving, or debt — until income minus assignments equals exactly zero. Borrowed from corporate budgeting (developed by Pete Pyhrr at Texas Instruments in the 1970s), it trades flexibility for total intentionality. It suits people who like detail and variable incomes that need month-by-month replanning; it exhausts people who don't.

do: Draft one zero-based month on paper: assign every expected dollar of next month's income a category until the unassigned remainder reads zero.

children.title: Envelope Method

learn.summary: Cash for each spending category goes into a labeled envelope; when an envelope is empty, that category is done for the month. It works by making abstract limits physical — behavioral research shows paying with cash registers a 'pain of paying' that cards and one-click checkouts are designed to remove. Modern versions use app-based virtual envelopes or multiple sub-accounts to get the same hard-edge feedback digitally.

do: Run a one-category experiment: put a cash amount for one leaky category (eating out, rideshares) in a physical envelope for two weeks and see how the constraint feels.
